Adult Island majors (Stegastes arcifrons) defending territories on the reef slope attain a maximum standard length of 13 cm [Li = 13 cm], a size that distinguishes them as one of the larger damselfishes in the eastern tropical Pacific. This ultimate length corresponds to a wet weight of 43.6 grams [Wwi = 43.6 grams], estimated from length-weight regressions fitted to a substantial series of field-collected individuals. The species exhibits a relatively slow somatic growth trajectory, with individuals taking several years to approach this asymptotic size, a pattern consistent with other long-lived pomacentrids that engage in prolonged nest-guarding and benthic care. Reproductive activity begins at a considerably smaller size, with the standard length at puberty measured at 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm], a size that marks the onset of gonadal maturation. The corresponding wet weight at puberty reaches approximately 2.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.5 grams], a threshold that signals the transition from a rapidly growing sub-adult to a reproductively capable individual undergoing full gonadal recrudescence. At this stage, juveniles undergo distinct allometric shifts in body plan, including complete fin ray ossification and the onset of scale formation. The extended growth interval between the pubertal size and the ultimate adult length suggests that resources are partitioned between continued somatic investment and the energetic demands of repeated spawning bouts over many seasons.

Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae of Stegastes arcifrons emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs that average 1 mm in diameter, and each prolarva carries a wet weight at birth of just 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. This minute initial mass underscores the highly fecund, dissociated reproductive strategy typical of the genus, wherein females produce large numbers of small offspring that embark on a pelagic larval phase. The lecithotrophic larvae remain dependent on endogenous yolk reserves for a brief window after eclosion, and under stable thermal conditions measured at 24.4 °C [T = 24.4 °C], the age at birth—the interval from egg fertilisation to hatching—is roughly 6 days [ab = roughly 6 days]. This rapid embryogenesis is comparable to that of other warm-water pomacentrids and is facilitated by the elevated metabolic rates sustained at these temperatures. Following chorion rupture and larval eclosion, the yolk-sac fry begin mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding within a day or two, marking the trophic switch to a diet of planktonic copepods and small zooplankton. The abbreviated egg incubation period reflects the selective pressures of the warm, oligotrophic waters these fish inhabit, where early hatching may reduce vulnerability to egg predators such as wrasse and invertebrate grazers.

Reproductive output in Stegastes arcifrons peaks during the warm season when water temperatures consistently reach 24.4 °C [T = 24.4 °C], conditions that promote rapid gametogenesis and high spawning frequency. Field observations indicate that a single, large territorial female can deposit up to 200 eggs per day [Ri = up to 200 eggs per day] during the height of the breeding period, sustained over multiple consecutive days before a brief refractory interval. This daily egg production, among the highest documented for eastern Pacific pomacentrids, is balanced by substantial mortality during the pelagic larval phase, with only a small fraction of the planktonic larvae surviving to settle on suitable reef habitat. Each batch of eggs is laid in a meticulously prepared nest site—a small depression on the reef substrate cleared of algae—where the male assumes sole guarding responsibility, fanning the clutch with his pectoral fins and aggressively repelling intruders. The breeding season can extend over several months, and individual females likely produce multiple clutches per season, although the exact number of annual spawning events has not been rigorously quantified for this species.

The lifespan of Stegastes arcifrons is notably extended for a fish of its body size, with individuals living up to approximately 30 years [am = up to approximately 30 years] at a mean annual water temperature of 24.4 °C [T = 24.4 °C]. This exceptional longevity, comparable to that of some large-bodied groupers, is remarkable given its modest ultimate size of 13 cm [Li = 13 cm] standard length and likely reflects the benefits of strong site fidelity, well-defended territories, and a relatively low predation risk once adulthood is attained. Senescence appears to be gradual, with older adults showing reduced condition factor and diminished reproductive output in their final years before natural mortality. The species' slow life history—characterised by a long lifespan, late maturation, and high annual fecundity—places it at the slower end of the fast-slow continuum for reef fishes, a strategy that may be advantageous in the stable, resource-predictable environments of the far eastern Pacific islands. Age determination from otolith microincrements confirms that individuals reaching the ultimate length of 13 cm [Li = 13 cm] are typically in their second decade of life, indicating a protracted period of near-asymptotic growth during which energy is partitioned primarily toward reproduction and territory maintenance rather than further somatic increase.

Comparing these life-history traits to those of the better-studied Chromis chromis provides a useful context for understanding the evolutionary constraints on Stegastes arcifrons. In the Mediterranean damselfish, maximum reproductive rates are similarly high, and analogous thermal dependencies have been documented, though the absolute daily egg output of approximately 200 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 200 eggs per day] measured at 24.4 °C [T = 24.4 °C] in the Island major represents an upper bound for the genus. The wet weight at puberty of 2.5 grams [Wwp = 2.5 grams] is reached when the fish attains a standard length of 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm], a point at which the first vitellogenic oocytes become visible in histological sections. By contrast, the transition from a neonate weighing only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] at hatching to a fully mature adult of 43.6 grams [Wwi = 43.6 grams] represents a mass increase of over 80,000-fold, underscoring the extreme disparity between batch fecundity and per-offspring investment typical of demersal-spawning pomacentrids. The cumulative effect of these life-history parameters—rapid embryogenesis, high fecundity, delayed maturation, and extreme longevity—positions Stegastes arcifrons as a successful, long-lived resident of eastern Pacific coral and rocky reefs, well adapted to the thermal regime of 24.4 °C that characterises its range.
